title: Colors of the year

lines: GREEN COMES DOWN, PURPLE GOES UP.
cards: In the back room of a church there's a cupboard full of cloth. Purple, folded on one shelf. White and gold on another.
A bright red. A tall stack of green. One week, someone takes the green cloth off the altar and the pulpit, folds it away, and hangs up purple.
The minister's stole changes to match. Nobody makes an announcement. But someone who comes every week can glance at the front and know, without a calendar, what time of year it is.

teach.b: Churches that keep the church calendar mark its seasons with colors, on the altar, the pulpit, and what the clergy wear.
Customs vary, and Orthodox churches have color customs of their own, but a pattern you may meet runs like this.
First, purple: Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas, and Lent, the weeks of turning back before Easter.
Purple is a king's color, and the Gospels give it a hard edge: before the crucifixion, Mark says, the soldiers "clothed him with purple," and mocked him as a king.
So some readers hear in purple both waiting for a king and sorrow over what was done to one. Some churches use blue in Advent instead. Next, white, for Christmas and Easter.
At the empty tomb, Mark says the women "saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment."
White for the feasts, for joy, for light.

teach.h: RED: TONGUES LIKE AS OF FIRE.
teach.b: Then red, for Pentecost, when the Spirit came on the disciples: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."

Red is fire, and some churches use it on the days that remember martyrs too. Last, green, for the long stretches between the big feasts, which some churches call ordinary time: the green season of day one hundred twenty.

Green is growth, plain and slow. Ecclesiastes gives the whole cupboard its reason: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." In these churches, the year isn't one long gray line.

how: Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and other churches that keep the church calendar change the colors of altar cloths and clergy vestments with the seasons, often purple for Advent and Lent, white for Christmas and Easter, red for Pentecost and green for ordinary time; Orthodox churches have their own color customs.

games.q: what does “colors of the year” mean?
o: colors that mark the seasons of the church year
colors that show a priest's rank in the church
colors each church picks to match its own style

p: Pentecost: tongues like as of fire

s: purple marks the seasons of waiting and turning before Christmas and Easter
Advent and Lent, in churches that keep the church calendar.
every church uses exactly the same colors

games.q: it's Pentecost Sunday, the day the church remembers the Spirit coming on the disciples. you're setting out the cloth for the altar. which color?
games.why: red, for fire: "there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."

practice: Find something in the color of the church season, a scarf, a ribbon, a leaf, or, if you don't know the season, something green, the color of the ordinary stretches.
Let it stand for the season you yourself are in: waiting, celebrating, on fire, or just growing slowly. If you pray, you can say the line from Ecclesiastes: to every thing there is a season.

wordCard.voice: Colors of the year. Purple, white, red and green, marking the seasons of the church calendar so the time of year can be seen.

orig.note: Greek: purple, the cloth the soldiers put on Jesus in Mark 15:17.

carryVoice: Your line: time has colors. Each season, its own. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.
